lede: A blind-critic loop on the overworld's art. Each round: builders change something, a FRESH Opus 5 critic that has never seen this project compares our frames against real FFIX-reimagined screenshots without being told which is which, and its reasons become the next round's work. The bar is artistry, not numeric similarity. NOTE ON VIEWPOINTS: rounds 0-3 shot low corridor/closeup views; round 4 switched to the four standing views (meadow/gate/gorge/vista) and no instrument caught the change — the user did, from this page. The FOLIAGE loop below therefore shoots FIVE fixed views including the restored low closeup, and they do not change again.

rounds.title: Before — the starting point
rounds.when: 2026-08-04, after the three.js r128 to r185 upgrade
rounds.verdict: Ranked 3rd of 3, very high confidence. But the cause is narrow: not assets, not texture resolution, not colour taste - the lighting solve. Measured on matched ground patches, our lit-to-shadow ratio is 1.30:1 with saturation FLAT across the terminator; a golden-hour sun should be 2.5-4:1. In the critic's words: 'What A has is not a sun, it's an ambient multiplier with a slight gradient.'
deficits: PIPELINE: cast and contact shadows - fourteen houses, a dozen trees, a character, a whole cliff, and not one shadow on the ground
PIPELINE: a 3:1 key-to-fill ratio, with a warm key and cool ambient so shadows pick up sky rather than being the lit colour dimmed
PIPELINE: recover the tonal range - the whole frame lives between 0.13 and 0.71 luminance, no true black or white
CONTENT: vary the instanced dressing - rotation jitter, plus or minus 15% scale, 2-3 roof tints on the existing house asset
CONTENT: the blade layer visibly stops - push density and extend the fade so the ground does not change species mid-frame
DROPPED: lower the camera for a horizon - user ruling, the camera is set for the scale of world we want to explore

rounds.title: Content: near-field blade carpet scattered by distance
rounds.when: 2026-08-04 — partial; lane killed by a session limit mid-commit
rounds.verdict: Not separately judged — round 2's critic saw the camera-tilt frames instead.
deficits: Near-field detail +82% at the gate; blades scattered by DISTANCE rather than by material seam, because our detail peaked mid-frame while the references climb into the near field.

rounds.title: Camera: an aim tilt puts a horizon in frame for the first time
rounds.when: 2026-08-04 — shipped as default, ?owtilt=0 restores the old frame
rounds.verdict: Ranked 3rd and 4th of four (meadow above gorge). The gap is large and it is NOT mostly asset budget: the top four fixes are all TREATMENT. The critic's summary — 'light is currently a GLOBAL TINT rather than a DIRECTION: every surface got warmer, but nothing got occluded, so nothing has form. Fix that one thing before commissioning a single new asset.'
deficits: TREATMENT: cast shadows with one committed key direction — nothing casts one; largest single change available
ASSET: a near-field ground-detail tier, dense at the bottom of frame and thinning with distance — the current tuft is too sparse, too uniform, too spindly to read as ground cover

TREATMENT: the firepit is CLIPPED to pure white over ~60px with a bloom ~3x its plausible radius, over a circular gradient decal that does not follow the terrain and does not light the houses beside it
TREATMENT: depth fog / aerial perspective — the tan hill upper-right is as saturated and contrasty as grass three metres from camera
BROKEN (gorge): two hard-edged grey rectangles over the sky top-left — 'reads as a crash artefact'. INDEPENDENTLY CORROBORATES the camera lane's own unfixed 'pale grey rectangle upper-left'
BROKEN (gorge): plateau grass upper-right blows to pale blue-white with a STRAIGHT-LINE terminator — a slope does not do that; fog volume or bloom threshold
BROKEN (gorge): several ridge trees render pure white/unlit while their neighbours are green
TREATMENT: anti-aliasing — roof ridgelines and canopy edges are stair-stepped at 1x
ASSET: water shader and shoreline — flat opaque planes butting terrain on a clean edge, no shallows, no wet band

rounds.title: Treatment: the sun gets a direction, the distance gets air, the Heartlight gets a light
rounds.when: 2026-08-04 — shipped as default; ?owkey= ?owenv= ?owsun= ?owbounce= ?owemit= ?owhearth= ?grade_d= ?tone=off sweep every number in it
rounds.verdict: Not yet judged — built against rounds 1 and 2, which named the same deficit twice. LIT-TO-SHADOW, measured on the engine's OWN shadow pass (tools/ow_ratio.mjs, maskrel 0.5, four viewpoints): gate 2.40 -> 4.24, meadow 1.77 -> 3.29, vista 1.79 -> 3.92, gorge 1.58 -> 4.33, against 2.5-4:1 for golden hour. And the terminator is a HUE now, not only a level: mean (g-r) on the shadowed pixels was -2.4/-0.3/-0.2/-1.7 (flat) and is +4.0/+9.3/+9.4/+11.7 (blue-green), while the lit side goes further warm on all four.
deficits: SHIPPED: the fill was the ENVIRONMENT, not the fog — a warm cos^12 sun cap supplied about half the ambient irradiance and gave the shadow side the lit side's hue. The fill is now plain sky radiance at 0.35, the cap 4.5 -> 0.30, the key x2.4, and NeutralToneMapping (hue-preserving; the 2026-08-02 ruling that rejected tone mapping was measured on ACES and AgX and still holds for both)

SHIPPED: aerial perspective's third half — the far band now LOSES CHROMA toward its own luminance, graded by depth. Measured on the two daylight references, their saturation RISES toward the camera (FAR 0.30/0.35 -> NEAR 0.48/0.49) while ours was flat and roughly double

SHIPPED: the fog was aimed at the sky's horizon band, but the camera tilt put four ridge rings (luma 0.24-0.60) in front of it, so far terrain faded to a value BRIGHTER than the thing behind it. Re-aimed at the ring band: the gorge's washed far slope L50 0.711 -> 0.668 and GAINS saturation 0.119 -> 0.142

SHIPPED: the 'firepit' is the HEARTLIGHT, and it now casts light — one point light at the plinth, emissive ceiling 9 -> 3.4, overworld bloom radius 0.30 -> 0.15. The critic's third claim was checked and is WRONG: the 'circular gradient decal' is walk_emberbrook_green, the village green

DIAGNOSED, NOT A BUG: the gorge's 'straight-line terminator into overexposure' is the plateau CREST — real terrain — with the slope beyond it washed by fog. Fog off moves that patch L50 0.711 -> 0.593, the tone curve moves it 0.738 -> 0.711; it was fog, and it is now largely gone
STILL OPEN: the two grey rectangles over the gorge sky. Untouched this round
STILL OPEN (CONTENT lane): the near-field blade carpet reads as oversized at the gate and meadow cameras, and the frame's near-band saturation is 0.70-0.79 against the references' 0.48-0.49

rounds.title: Lighting: the sun gets a direction — and the picture gets WORSE
rounds.when: 2026-08-04 03:10 — a regression, caught by the blind critic
rounds.verdict: Ranked LAST of four, below the frame it replaced. THE LOOP'S MOST IMPORTANT ROUND: the builder hit its target (lit:shadow 1.6-2.4:1 -> 3.3-4.3:1, real hue on the terminator) and the frame regressed - one garish amber band, oversized grass reading as scribble, a blown Heartlight. The builder MEASURED both faults (near-band saturation 0.70-0.79 vs the refs' 0.48-0.49; 'the blade carpet reads oversized') and shipped anyway, because its target was a ratio. The critic - blind, fresh, with no access to the numbers - ranked it below its predecessor.
deficits: THE LESSON: a number improved and the picture got worse. The user's rule, vindicated: 'the goal is not to meet the reference numerically.' A ratio is a diagnostic; the frame is the deliverable.

rounds.title: The grade goes into the light; the artefacts get named
rounds.verdict: Ranked 4th of 4. The critic's headline: 'There is not one cast shadow in the entire frame… the houses have no lit side and no shade side. Four walls, one colour.' And its summary of two frames from the same build: 'A got a colour grade and B got a light.' It ALSO caught an over-correction I had missed after looking myself: the golden grade is past the point where hue distinctions survive.
deficits: FIXED: the grade was multiplying EVERY near pixel by a warm colour - a global tint arriving through the post pass, the exact defect the lighting round existed to remove. Now weighted by each pixel's own luminance: full on lit surfaces, nothing in shadow.
FIXED: the key's blue channel was closed. (1.0,0.70,0.42) at 2.4x turned grass albedo into yellow - NO lit surface could read green whatever its albedo.

FIXED: HALF THE BLADE CARPET WAS RENDERING BLACK - three.js's DOUBLE_SIDED normal flip negating the blade's authored up-normal on back faces, with yaw uniform over 2pi, so ~half of 177k instances pointed at the dirt.

FIXED: the grey rectangles were THE AO PASS'S OWN DEPTH BUFFER. GTAOPass draws its prepass with scene.overrideMaterial = MeshNormalMaterial, which carries neither the leaf atlas nor its alphaTest - so every alpha-cut foliage card writes its WHOLE QUAD into the g-buffer, and a camera-facing billboard is axis-aligned in screen space by construction. The aerial grade then read 11 m where the picture shows a 233 m ridge.
FIXED: the 'unlit white trees' and the 'missing skybox' were ONE NUMBER - the fog was aimed at a colour between the two FURTHEST ridge rings while the terrain's skyline is drawn against ring 0.
REFUSED: going all the way to the refs' near-band saturation was tried and the frame got worse - milky, flat trees, amber graded away. Stopped at 0.60-0.70 and said so.

rounds.title: The houses were too small to cast a shadow the sun could draw
rounds.verdict: THE ROUND THAT PAID FOR THE LOOP. Four rounds of critique named 'no directional light'; chasing it directly produced one regression and one cleanup. The cause was never the light. THREE blind critics said 'the character is roughly one house tall' from looking, and a shadow lane derived the same thing from geometry: cottages 2.6 m tall and 2.9 m WIDE, height:width below 1, so at 34 degrees the shadow barely outran the footprint that threw it. The only object in the frame with a visible shadow was the character - the only thing taller than it was wide.
deficits: ridge height 1.60u -> 3.70u; 1.10x the character -> 2.65x (2.97x to the chimney cap)
height:width 1.10 -> 1.39; shadow at 34 degrees 2.4u from a 1.5u footprint -> 5.7u from a 2.76u footprint
Gained eave board, steep gable, gable-end chimney, person-sized door, stone footing that reaches BELOW the lowest footprint corner so a house on a slope is not cut by a straight line

BROKE AND FIXED: a house landed ON the 'Enter Emberbrook' portal - the old road-clearance push was RADIAL, which for a house bearing along the road walks it DOWN the road. Every gate was green with it there; only the frame showed it.
BROKE AND FIXED: Dellhollow lost a third of its stations (11 -> 7) to wider terrace pads. Back to 11.
OPEN, needs the coordinator: the Heartlight is now a garden ornament among 4u houses. Geometry and play3d's point light are both hard-coded at village_h+1.34 and must move in one commit.
NOT TRIED - RAN OUT OF NIGHT: ground de-tiling and the water shoreline. Both are terrain-material work sitting one step from the grade.

rounds.title: Golden hour is a warm key AND a blue fill — we had applied the key to both
rounds.verdict: The critic's three-line summary is the whole diagnosis: 'The light has one colour instead of two. The ground is a colour instead of a surface. Objects rest on the terrain instead of being bedded into it. Fix those three and these frames move most of the distance without a single new building model. Add ten new props first and they will not move at all.' By eye after the fix: every cottage has a warm lit wall and a violet-cool shaded wall, roof planes separate, the grass is green again.
deficits: FIXED: warm key kept, ambient/fill made blue-violet. Frame saturation .651/.584/.478/.456 -> .540/.496/.411/.360; meadow b-r -.357 -> -.284; grass (184,170,70) -> (197,180,111).

FIXED, and three earlier rounds had swept the wrong knob: THE WINDOW WAS NEVER THE EMISSIVE. At owemit=0.02 with bloom OFF the pane still read (254,215,193) - new_mat's use_vcol default handed Base Color to COLOR_0, so the pane had a near-WHITE ALBEDO. Dark base + use_vcol=False, and only then did the knob work.

REFUTED: 'the floating building' was not floating. Measured with a new SIM.pick raycast at the critic's own pixels - the footing's underside sits at y 25.77 against terrain at 26.19-26.33, BURIED 0.4-0.6u. A 4px scan of all four frames found no downward-facing first hit on any building; Blender agreed (15 buildings, 0 with a positive gap). The 'daylight beneath' was downhill ground passing in front.

BUT THE MISREAD NAMED A REAL DEFECT: the footing spanned the whole corner spread, so on a 1.3u-spread station it grew to wall height - a 1.5u block of stone with no contact shading. emberbrook_house_slope_u 1.3 -> 0.47.
REFUTED: the 'blob shadow with no caster' is pixel-identical with every veg_ mesh hidden, and at __shadowTune(0) resolves into a chimney stack. Real caster, smeared by texel size.
GOT WORSE, recorded not smoothed: the gorge's far plateau is paler and cooler - the raised fill lands on everything and that frame has the most sky-lit open ground.
CAUGHT BY EYE BEFORE SHIPPING: the first bedding ring used an untinted DIRT and arrived as CREAM - a bright halo round every house, the exact decal read it exists to prevent.

rounds.title: r11 — the campfire was two additive sprites over 1.0, and the depth ramp had never run
rounds.verdict: Both of the round's own tests passed (greens off yellow, real darks) and the blind rank did not move: D>C>B>A. The cool sky-fill and the crushed darks were each correct and wrong together — shadows went blue-purple in the meadow, plum across the gorge road. The critic: 'A is charm without light.'

rounds.title: r12 — the plum was a literal violet fill, and haze was sRGB in a linear pass
rounds.verdict: Three arithmetic defects: fill [0.42,0.44,1.00] IS a violet; the depth ramp normalised over 149m in 40-60m scenes (far MORE saturated than near, delta -0.084); hazeCol landed a stop and a half up so more haze made distance whiter. Shadow hue moved 273°→41° — and the target was neither (refs sit cool ~200-230°). Rank unchanged.

rounds.title: r13 — we matched the numbers and lost the picture
rounds.verdict: Best instrument of the loop (material classifier split by each material's own luminance quartiles) overturned three settled beliefs — a reference shadow is MORE saturated than its lit neighbour; ZERO reference pixels sit under L 0.10; violet was wrong for being magenta, not for being cool. Then the critic called the result washed out: the classifier measured grass and stone, and the HOUSES were never a measured class. 'A statistic constrains a distribution and says nothing about the relationships inside the frame.'

rounds.title: r14 — the grade's missing cool half, and the roofs that went blue to feed a histogram
rounds.verdict: The grade only ever had its warm half written (eight rounds of warming the light, shade left at vec3(1.0)); key:fill 7.6→17.5. The classifier was deleting 36% of the roof pixels it measured. Black slivers gone (2648→0). Then framespread wanted a cool sector, the roofs were the cheapest object to paint, and the critic called them 'the single worst decision in A' — the references' cool is river, mist and sky. A histogram does not care which object supplies a bin. Loop paused here by the user; re-scoped to FOLIAGE.

rounds.title: FOLIAGE 1 (grass & bushes) — a population of plants, not a surface treatment
rounds.verdict: CRITIC PENDING. Baseline critique ranked r3's old blade carpet ABOVE both r14 plates ('set size aside and it is the right family of solution') and named the gap: the references' vegetation is a population of individual clumped plants that breaks every silhouette and every seam; ours is a surface treatment applied to terrain. This round: clumped instanced tufts at 1/3 r3 scale, fringe bands on every path edge and silhouette, hemispherical bushes, one shared material fix (roughness, translucency, highlight clamp).

rounds.title: TREES 1 — crowns, not cauliflower
rounds.verdict: CRITIC PENDING. User: 'the trees are even more far off the mark than the grass.' This round: crown rebuilt as one shaped hull with leaf-scale ragged edges (was large cards clustered into lobes), foliage_atlas value ramp re-targeted (narrow value, wide hue — the near-black cores were baked into the art), second species + 0.6-1.5x scale ramp for the gorge ridge.
